title: Learning a Persons Backstory Creates a Powerful Connection
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that leaders who take time to learn even a small slice of a colleague's or client's personal history deepen the relationship in ways that pure professional courtesy cannot match. The piece contends that people rarely go above and beyond for leaders who don't genuinely know them, and offers a list of sample questions leaders can use to draw out someone's formative experiences, mentors, and turning points. It also notes that this exchange works best when reciprocal — once a team member has shared their story, a leader who is willing to share a bit of their own history in return strengthens the bond further. The article frames curiosity about backstories as a defining marker of relational commitment.
points: Learning even a small part of someone's personal history instantly deepens a working relationship.
Team members rarely perform at their best for leaders who don't genuinely know them.
Backstory conversations reveal what people value, often more directly than asking about values outright.
The article offers a set of sample questions leaders can use to draw out someone's formative experiences.
Reciprocating with some of the leader's own history, at the right moment, strengthens the bond further.
quotes: Knowing the backstory of another person’s life instantly deepens the relationship.
Team members don’t go above and beyond for leaders who don’t really know or understand them.
By exploring backstories, leaders learn what people value and how they think about themselves.
It is nearly impossible for anyone to explain their backstory without pointing directly at what they value and cherish.
This disclosure binds leaders and team members together and strengthens their relationships.
Being curious about the backstories of team members, clients, and friends defines leaders as committed to the relationship in a way very few other inquiries can match.
